records.sourceFile: Nutritional and Supplementation Strategies to Prevent and Attenuate Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage- a Brief Review.pdf

paper.citation: Harty PS, Cottet ML, Malloy JK, Kerksick CM. Nutritional and Supplementation Strategies to Prevent and Attenuate Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage: a Brief Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2019;5:1.
paper.abstract: This brief narrative review summarises nutritional and supplementation strategies that have been studied for exercise-induced muscle damage, grouped by nutrient source. It states that many strategies have been tested with varying results, and it focuses on acute damaging-exercise studies. The authors state that effective strategies matter to athletes whose training quality and performance are affected by muscle damage.
paper.tldr: Several foods and supplements, including tart cherry, pomegranate, protease and chronic n-3 fatty acids, show some benefit for muscle damage symptoms, but results are mixed and often depend on the damaging exercise used. The review offers no firm dosing guidance.
paper.methods: Brief narrative review by four authors, organised into fruit, vegetable, herb, amino acid and protein, vitamin, and other supplement sections. Only strategies tested in at least two well-controlled studies were included, acute damaging-exercise studies were the focus, and oxidative stress outcomes were excluded. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: Chronic tart cherry juice or concentrate is described as effectively modulating muscle damage symptoms, and pomegranate juice as improving functional measures and reducing markers of damage in several studies. Protease supplements improved muscle function and soreness in some studies, but effects on biomarkers were less clear. Vitamin D3 may improve outcomes, whereas vitamin D2 may increase damage in one study, and caffeine mainly reduces soreness rather than biomarkers.
paper.limitations: The review is brief and selective, and it describes no systematic search or risk-of-bias assessment. Some cited studies used damage protocols that the authors judged insufficient to produce a clear effect, and the authors note that the effects of combined strategies and the potency of many strategies in female participants remain unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes who need quick recovery between damaging sessions could trial tart cherry or pomegranate products, and staff can track soreness and function to judge individual response. The authors warn that long-term use of some nutrients may impair training adaptations, so chronic use should be weighed against the need for recovery. Staff should not assume that any one supplement is proven, because the review rates many results as mixed.
paper.athleteDev: For athletes who must recover quickly between damaging training or competition, the review describes some supplements, such as tart cherry and protease, as promising for soreness and muscle function. The review states that these effects are inconsistent, and long-term use may blunt training adaptations, so they should be trialled and monitored rather than assumed to improve performance.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It covers recovery from exercise-induced soreness and muscle damage in healthy or active people, and it does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play.

records.sourceFile: Nutritional interventions to improve sleep in team sport athletes - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Gratwicke M, Miles KH, Pyne DB, Pumpa KL, Clark B. Nutritional Interventions to Improve Sleep in Team-Sport Athletes: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2021;13:1586.
paper.abstract: The authors review nutritional interventions for sleep quality and quantity in team-sport athletes. They found few athlete studies and report that selected interventions improve sleep in general populations, with dose, source and timing still to be defined for athletes.
paper.tldr: Sleep nutrition evidence in athletes is limited to four small studies with mixed results. Most supporting evidence comes from healthy adults and poor sleepers, so the timing and doses in this review should be trialled with individual athletes.
paper.methods: Narrative review with a semi-systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL, EMBASE, SPORTDiscus and Google Scholar to November 2020. Athlete studies were prioritised, and healthy adult and poor-sleeper trials were included because athlete data are scarce.
paper.findings: The four athlete studies were mixed: high-carbohydrate drinks during intensified training reduced total sleep time by 19 minutes in 10 cyclists (Table 2), a high-glycemic-index evening meal gave a non-significant 26.5-minute increase in 8 basketball players, 40 g alpha-lactalbumin had no effect in 6 track cyclists, and beetroot juice improved PSQI sleep quality in 30 male athletes. In non-athletes, a high-glycemic-index meal after evening exercise increased total sleep time by 62 minutes in 10 healthy active males, two kiwifruit an hour before bed added 55 minutes in 24 poor sleepers, 20 g alpha-lactalbumin added 55 minutes in 10 healthy males, and tart cherry juice added 29 to 39 minutes in two trials.
paper.limitations: Only four athlete studies were included, with 6 to 30 participants each, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment is reported. The text and tables disagree on several attributions, so Table 1 values are used here: the text assigns cycling to refs 21 and 22 and basketball to ref 23, while Table 1 lists ref 22 (Daniel) as basketball, ref 23 (Shamloo) as unspecified male athletes and ref 24 (MacInnis) as track cyclists; Table 2 labels Daniel as ref 24 and Inagawa as ref 30; and the tart cherry discussion swaps the healthy-adult (Howatson, ref 27) and insomnia (Pigeon, ref 31) studies. The text also does not discuss the athlete carbohydrate study that Table 2 shows reducing total sleep time.
paper.practicalImplications: For an athlete with sleep trouble after late training, competition or travel, the authors suggest options such as a high-glycemic-index meal 2 to 4 hours before bed, 3 g of glycine before bed, kiwifruit, or tart cherry juice, based mainly on non-athlete data. Their suggested 20 to 40 g alpha-lactalbumin 2 hours before bed is the protocol that showed no effect in the only athlete trial. The review also advises avoiding caffeine, alcohol and excess fluid before sleep.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not measure performance outcomes that would support a performance claim. Its sleep findings come from small athlete samples and from non-athletes.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport or injury recovery, and it excluded participants with concussion. It cannot be used to set a sleep or nutrition plan during concussion or post-injury rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: Nutritional modulation of sleep latency, duration, and efficiency - A randomized, repeated-measures, double-blind deception study.pdf

paper.citation: Langan-Evans C, Hearris MA, Gallagher C, Long S, Thomas C, Moss AD, et al. Nutritional Modulation of Sleep Latency, Duration, and Efficiency: A Randomized, Repeated-Measures, Double-Blind Deception Study. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2023;55(2):289-300.
paper.abstract: Randomized, repeated-measures, double-blind crossover study in 16 healthy adults testing whether a blend of tryptophan, glycine, magnesium, tart cherry powder and L-theanine improves sleep under free-living conditions. Participants were told the study was about fat oxidation; 75% did not identify sleep as the true outcome. The blend shortened sleep onset latency, increased total sleep time and sleep efficiency, and reduced morning sleepiness compared with placebo.
paper.tldr: In 16 healthy non-athlete adults, a pre-bed blend of tryptophan, glycine, magnesium, tart cherry and L-theanine helped them fall asleep about 24 minutes faster and sleep about 22 minutes longer over 3 nights than placebo. It has not been tested in athletes or for performance.
paper.methods: After a 3-day familiarization period to record habitual sleep, diet, activity and light exposure, participants completed 3-day intervention and placebo trials in random order, 4 days apart, taking opaque pills 2 h before bed. Sleep was measured with wrist actigraphy (MotionWatch 8), the Consensus Sleep Diary and the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale, and diet was replicated using weighed food records and photographs with 100% reported compliance. Conditions were compared with paired t-tests or Wilcoxon tests, and urine metabolomics were analysed in a random subgroup of 8.
paper.findings: Sleep onset latency was 16 +/- 6 min with the blend versus 40 +/- 25 min with placebo (P = 0.002, ES 1.29), total sleep time 422 vs 400 min (P = 0.01, ES 0.55), and sleep efficiency 83.3% vs 80.9% (P = 0.03, ES 0.48). Wake after sleep onset (49 vs 51 min) and time in bed did not differ, and morning but not evening sleepiness was lower with the blend (P = 0.02). In the 8-person metabolomic subgroup, urinary 6-sulfatoxymelatonin and D-serine were higher and L-glutamic acid lower with the blend.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, not athletes, and each trial lasted only 3 nights, so longer-term effects are unknown. Actigraphy cannot assess sleep stages, the blend cannot isolate individual ingredients, and magnesium status was not measured. Half the sample were poor sleepers by PSQI and 14 of 16 had short or inefficient sleep by actigraphy at baseline, which may not reflect well-rested athletes; the study was funded by Science in Sport and one author consults for the company, which the authors state had no role in the study.
paper.practicalImplications: For staff working with athletes who report trouble falling asleep, this blend taken 2 h before bed is one option with controlled evidence of shorter sleep onset over a few nights in healthy young adults. Any use with athletes should be checked for anti-doping certification and monitored individually, since the study did not include athletes.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured no training, performance or recovery outcomes, so it cannot show that the sleep changes improve athletic performance. The authors' links to exercise performance are discussion only.
paper.rtp: The study did not involve injured athletes or rehabilitation, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Overview of the impact of sleep monitoring on optimal performance, immune system function and injury risk reduction in athletes - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Nobari H, Banihashemi M, Saedmocheshi S, Prieto-González P, Oliveira R. Overview of the impact of sleep monitoring on optimal performance, immune system function and injury risk reduction in athletes: a narrative review. Sci Prog. 2023;106(4):1-18.
paper.abstract: This narrative review examines how sleep quantity and quality affect performance, recovery, immune function and injury risk in athletes, and how sleep can be monitored. The authors state that athletes may experience lower sleep quality and quantity than is needed. They describe questionnaires, sleep diaries, actigraphy and polysomnography as monitoring options, with nutrition and bedtime routines as improvement strategies.
paper.tldr: The review argues that athletes often sleep less and worse than they need and that sleep should be monitored alongside training load. Its specific injury and performance figures are attached to mismatched or missing references, so treat it as a general overview, not a source of numbers.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, selection criteria or quality appraisal. It covers sleep physiology, hormones and immune function, sex differences, sleep monitoring tools (questionnaires, diaries, actigraphy and polysomnography), nutrition and supplements, and sleep-hygiene tips.
paper.findings: The review's clearest sourced content is on monitoring: it reports that actigraphy showed 81 to 90% agreement and 81 to 92% sensitivity against polysomnography in athletes, that software thresholds change its bias, and that it performs poorly in people with fragmented sleep. It also states that sleeping under 8 hours was linked to a 65% higher injury risk in 122 athletes, that adolescent athletes sleeping under 8 hours were injured 1.7 times as often, and that extending sleep to about 8.4 hours improved endurance performance; these are not established findings here, because the first and third cite references on consumer sleep devices and the second has no citation. It lists tryptophan, melatonin (5 to 8 mg) and other supplements in Table 1, noting no demonstrated benefit for valerian or L-theanine.
paper.limitations: The paper does not describe how sources were selected or appraised. Several claims cite references that do not match them: the 65% injury figure cites a review of consumer sleep devices (ref 22), the soccer sleep-deprivation and injury claim cites a paper on betatrophin in type 1 diabetes (ref 23), the endurance sleep-extension result cites a review of consumer trackers (ref 26), and the sex-difference figures cite supplement and meal studies (refs 43, 44). Several passages are garbled, including the sex-difference sentence, the kiwifruit paragraph, 'octopography' for actigraphy, 'I require 12 hours of sleep every night' in Table 2, and a nap limit of 'half an afternoon', and the conclusion mentions wearable ultrasound monitors that the body text does not discuss.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can track sleep alongside training load, using low-cost questionnaires such as the Hooper index sleep item or sleep diaries routinely and research-grade actigraphy for multi-day tracking. General sleep-hygiene habits the review lists include a consistent bedtime and wake time, a dark, cool and quiet room, no screens in bed, avoiding caffeine close to bedtime, and avoiding late-afternoon or evening naps. The review's injury-risk and performance numbers should not be used to set policy without checking the original studies.
paper.athleteDev: The review states that short sleep is linked to lower speed, anaerobic power and attention, so performance staff can monitor sleep next to training load when planning sessions. It gives no validated thresholds, and it notes that smartphone sleep apps still need validation.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport or injury clearance. It notes that athletes may need extra sleep to recover from injuries caused by intense training, but it gives no sleep target or criteria for return to play.
